arXiv:1704.02961v1 [q-bio.PE] 10 Apr 2017

A nonlocal model of epidemic network with nonlimited transmission: Global existence and uniqueness

E.Logak, I.Passat Address: Université de Cergy-Pontoise, Departement de Mathématiques et Laboratoire AGM (UMR CNRS 8088), 2 avenue A. Chauvin, 95302 Cergy–Pontoise Cedex, France Email address: elisabeth.logak@u-cergy.fr, isabelle.passat@u-cergy.fr
Abstract.

Following [11], we consider a nonlinear SIS-type nonlocal system describing the spread of epidemics on networks, assuming nonlimited transmission, We prove local existence of a unique solution for any diffusion coefficients and global existence in the case of equal diffusion coefficients. Next we study the asymptotic behaviour of the solution and show that the disease-free equilibrium (DFE) is linearly and globally asymptotically stable when the total mean population is small. Finally, we prove that the solution of the system converge to the D​F​EDFE.

Key words and phrases: 
epidemic models, patchy environments, nonlocal diffusion, complex networks
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B10, 35B36, 35C05, 35C07, 35K65, 35Q92

1. Introduction

In this paper, we consider the model proposed in [11] for the spread of epidemics on heterogeneous networks. It is formally derived from a discrete model proposed in [16], [17] by considering the degree as a continuous variable. Precisely, each node of the network corresponds to a patch of the metapopulation and is characterised by its degree x>0x>0. We assume that the network is described by a continuous labelling of the nodes and is characterized by a degree distribution with density p⁡(x)p(x). We assume that pp has compact support J=[0,xm​a​x]J=[0,x_{max}] with xm​a​x>0x_{max}>0 and satisfies the assumptions

(1.1) ∀x∈J,p⁡(x)≥0,p⁡(0)=0​ and ​∫0xm​a​xp⁡(x)​𝑑x=1\forall x\in J,\,\,\,\,p(x)\geq 0,\,\,p(0)=0\mbox{ and }\int_{0}^{x_{max}}p(x)\,dx=1\\

The condition p⁡(0)=0p(0)=0 corresponds to a connected network, with no isolated patch.

We restrict to the case of uncorrelated network. For any function ϕ:J→ℝ\phi:J\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with ϕ∈L1​(J,p⁡(x)​d​x)\phi\in L^{1}(J,p(x)dx), we denote by ⟨ϕ⟩∈ℝ\langle\phi\rangle\in\mathbb{R} its mean value on the network defined by

(1.2) ⟨ϕ⟩=∫0xm​a​xϕ⁡(x)​p​(x)​𝑑x.\langle\phi\rangle=\int_{0}^{x_{max}}\phi(x)\,p(x)dx.

We assume the following property

ϕ≥0​ on ​J,⟨ϕ⟩=0⇒ϕ=0​ on ​J.\phi\geq 0\mbox{ on }J,\,\,\,\langle\phi\rangle=0\,\,\,\Rightarrow\,\,\,\phi=0\mbox{ on }J.

We also assume that the first-order moment is finite and denote by m>0m>0 its value defined as

(1.3) m=⟨x⟩=∫0xm​a​xx​p​(x)​𝑑x.m=\langle x\rangle=\int_{0}^{x_{max}}x\,p(x)\,dx.

Let us denote by S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) (resp. I⁡(x,t)I(x,t)) the density of susceptible (resp. infected) individuals of degree x∈Jx\in J at time t≥0t\geq 0. In our model, their evolution in time is given by the solution of the following nonlinear and nonlocal system,

(C)​{∂S∂t=I⁡(μ−β0​S)−DS​(S−xm​s​(t)),x∈J,t>0∂I∂t=I⁡(−μ+β0​S)−DI​(I−xm​i​(t)),x∈J,t>0S⁡(x,0)=S0​(x),x∈JI⁡(x,0)=I0​(x),x∈J(C)\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcll}\vskip 1.99168pt\displaystyle{\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}}&=&I(\mu-\beta_{0}S)-D_{S}(S-\displaystyle{\frac{x}{m}s(t)}),&x\in J,\,t>0\\ \vskip 1.42262pt\displaystyle{\frac{\partial I}{\partial t}}&=&I(-\mu+\beta_{0}S)-D_{I}(I-\displaystyle{\frac{x}{m}i(t)}),&x\in J,\,t>0\\ S(x,0)&=&S_{0}(x),&x\in J\\ I(x,0)&=&I_{0}(x),&x\in J\end{array}\right.\

with s⁡(t)s(t) and i⁡(t)i(t) given by

(1.4) ∀t>0,s(t)=⟨S(.,t)⟩,i(t)=⟨I(.,t)⟩.\forall t>0,\,\,\,\,\,\,s(t)=\langle S(.,t)\rangle,\,\,\,\,\,\,i(t)=\langle I(.,t)\rangle.

Here, DS,DI>0D_{S},D_{I}>0 are the diffusion coefficients and the constant μ>0\mu>0 is the recovery rate of the epidemics. We also define the total density of individuals of degree x∈Jx\in J at time t≥0t\geq 0 by

(1.5) N⁡(x,t)=S⁡(x,t)+I⁡(x,t).N(x,t)=S(x,t)+I(x,t).

In this paper, we deal with the case of nonlimited transmission and always assume that the transmission rate is a constant β0>0\beta_{0}>0. The companion paper [11] is devoted to the analysis of the model under the assumption of limited transmission, where

β=β0N⁡(x,t).\beta=\frac{\beta_{0}}{N(x,t)}.

We’ll see later that this assumption critically affects the results about equilibria.

The system (C)(C) is formally derived from the discrete SIS metapopulation model proposed in [16, 17, 18]. We refer the reader to [11] for a precise presentation of the discrete model.

Many recent papers have investigated dynamic processes on complex networks using the tools and methods of statistical physics (see [13] for a survey). In particular, epidemic networks have recently attracted a lot of attention both from modelling and practical and from theoretical viewpoint (see [14] and [9] for an introduction and [15] for a recent review).

This paper and its companion paper [11] originated from a series of papers by R.Pastor-Satorras, A.Vespignani, V. Collizza ([1], [2], [3]) which focuses on the propagation of epidemics in ”metapopulation”, a concept introduced to describe a population in which individuals are spatially distributed in patches forming subpopulations. Hence the metapopulation is naturally mapped onto a network, where nodes correspond to patches of subpopulations that migrate along the edges. The transmission of the epidemics takes place in each patch, whose population is composed of susceptible and infected individuals. Following these works, J. Saldana proposed in [16] and [17] a discrete model for the propagation of epidemics in a heterogeneous network, with the additional feature that reaction and diffusion processes take place simultaneously, allowing him to derive a time-continuous model. We propose to consider a continuous version, where both time and degree take values in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}. We claim that the resulting model is retaining the main features of the discrete ones, while simplifying the analysis and improving some of the results. Namely, we prove rigorously global existence and uniqueness results for system (C)(C). Besides, we establish in [12] the existence of a threshold for the existence of an endemic equilibrium and its stability, which depends on the whole degree distribution pp, and not just on its maximum value as was obtained on the discrete model.

The plan of the paper is the following. In section 2, we show that the system (C)(C) is well-posed for any couple of strictly positive diffusion coefficients (DI,DS)(D_{I},D_{S}) and with nonnegative smooth initial data. In the case of equal diffusion coefficients, we prove that the solution is global in time. The result is obtained using fixed point methods and apriori estimates on the solutions. In section 3, we investigate the linear stability of the disease-free equilibrium (DFE) and prove that for small enough n0n_{0}, it is also globally asymptotically stable. Next in section 4, we prove that if n0n_{0} small enough, the functions (S,I)(S,I) converge to the DFE.

3. Existence and linear stability of (D​F​E)(DFE)

In this section, we consider equilibrium solutions to system (C). Hence we look for nonnegative functions (S∗​(x),I∗​(x))(S^{*}(x),I^{*}(x)) which satisfy system (C∗)(C^{*}) on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}

(C∗)​{I​(x)∗​(μ−β0​S​(x)∗)=DS​(S​(x)∗−xm​s∗)I​(x)∗​(−μ+β0​S​(x)∗)=DI​(I​(x)∗−xm​i∗).(C^{*})\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcll}I(x)^{*}(\mu-\beta_{0}S(x)^{*})&=&D_{S}(S(x)^{*}-\frac{x}{m}s^{*})\\ I(x)^{*}(-\mu+\beta_{0}S(x)^{*})&=&D_{I}(I(x)^{*}-\frac{x}{m}i^{*}).\end{array}\right.

with

(3.1) s∗=∫0xm​a​xS∗​(x)​p​(x)​𝑑x​ and ​i∗=∫0xm​a​xI∗​(x)​p​(x)​𝑑x.s^{*}=\int_{0}^{x_{max}}S^{*}(x)p(x)dx\mbox{ and }i^{*}=\int_{0}^{x_{max}}I^{*}(x)p(x)dx.

The disease-free and endemic equilibria are defined as follows.

Definition 1.

For a given n0>0n_{0}>0, any equilibrium solution such that <N∗​(x)>=n0<N^{*}(x)>=n_{0} is of one of the two following types,

  • •

    The disease-free equilibrium (DFE), given by

    ∀x≥0,I∗​(x)=0,S∗​(x)=n0​xm,\forall x\geq 0,\,\,\,I^{*}(x)=0,\,\,\,S^{*}(x)=n_{0}\frac{x}{m},\,\,\,
  • •

    An endemic equilibrium (EE), which is a nonnegative solution (S∗​(x),I∗​(x))(S^{*}(x),I^{*}(x)) such that there exists x0>0x_{0}>0 with I∗​(x0)>0I^{*}(x_{0})>0.

Let us remark there always exists a (D​F​E)(DFE).

3.1. Necessary condition of linear stability

Let (S∗​(x),I∗​(x))(S^{*}(x),I^{*}(x)) be an equilibrium solution to system (C)(C), with s∗=<S∗>s^{*}=<S^{*}>, i∗=<I∗>i^{*}=<I^{*}> and n0=s∗+i∗n_{0}=s^{*}+i^{*}. The linearized system around (S∗​(x),I∗​(x))(S^{*}(x),I^{*}(x)) is given for all x>0x>0 by

(L)​{∂f∂t=−β​I∗​(x)​f+(μ−β​S∗)​g−DS​(f−xm​∫0xm​a​xf⁡(x,t)​p​(x)​dx)∂g∂t=β​I∗​(x)​f+(−μ+β​S∗)​g−DI​(g−xm​∫0xm​a​xg⁡(x,t)​p​(x)​dx),(L)\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcr}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=&-\beta I^{*}(x)f+(\mu-\beta S^{*})g-D_{S}(f-\frac{x}{m}\int_{0}^{x_{max}}f(x,t)p(x)dx)\\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}&=&\beta I^{*}(x)f+(-\mu+\beta S^{*})g-D_{I}(g-\frac{x}{m}\int_{0}^{x_{max}}g(x,t)p(x)dx),\end{array}\right.

with given initial data (f⁡(x,0),g⁡(x,0))=(f0​(x),g0​(x))(f(x,0),g(x,0))=(f_{0}(x),g_{0}(x)), which are 2 functions from ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} to ℝ\mathbb{R} such that

∫0xm​a​x|f0​(x)|p⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞,∫0xm​a​x|g0​(x)|p⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞.\int_{0}^{x_{max}}|f_{0}(x)|p(x)dx<\infty,\,\,\,\int_{0}^{x_{max}}|g_{0}(x)|p(x)dx<\infty.

We make the assumption that f0,g0:ℝ+→ℝf_{0},g_{0}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} are C1C^{1} and satisfy

(3.2) ⟨f0⟩+⟨g0⟩=∫0xm​a​x(f0​(x)+g0​(x))​p​(x)​𝑑x=0.\langle f_{0}\rangle+\langle g_{0}\rangle=\int_{0}^{x_{max}}(f_{0}(x)+g_{0}(x))\,p(x)\,dx=0.

We define linear stability of (L)(L) as follows:

Definition 2.

(S∗,I∗)(S^{*},I^{*}) is linearly stable if and only if ∀x>0\forall x>0,

limt⟶∞f⁡(x,t)=limt⟶∞g⁡(x,t)=0,\lim_{t\longrightarrow\infty}f(x,t)=\lim_{t\longrightarrow\infty}g(x,t)=0,

where (f,g)(f,g) is the solution of (L)(L) with initial data (f0,g0)(f_{0},g_{0}).

We also established that any solution (f,g)(f,g) to (L)(L) with (f0,g0)(f_{0},g_{0}) satisfying (3.2) has the property that

(3.4) ∀t≥0,H(t)=⟨f(.,t)⟩+⟨g(.,t)⟩=0.\forall t\geq 0,\,\,\,H(t)=\langle f(.,t)\rangle+\langle g(.,t)\rangle=0.
